Misunderstanding over local store's product causes controversyBy Mella McEwen
Staff Writer
January 19, 1998

An announcement that a kiosk in Midland Park Mall would be selling items made of hemp raised some eyebrows in Midland.

Called Simply Hemp, the kiosk sells items such as caps, hacky sack balls, fanny backs, hair scrunchies, bags and dufflebags through the month of May.

"I want to emphasize that these items are made from industrial hemp, not the hemp used to make marijuana," said Anita Teinert, an owner of the business, saying that she doesn't intend to promote the use of marijuana by selling products made of industrial hemp.

"I like poppyseed buns, but I don't use opium," she said. "I eat grapes but I don't drink wine."

Irma Castor, office administrator at the mall, said that Wednesday morning she got three complaint calls, including one from a woman who had discussed it with members of her Bible Study class that morning.

"They were adamant," she recalled. "They said that right now we're in a war against drugs and we don't need to do anything that will make our kids think we think marijuana is OK," she said.

She said that when Ms. Teinert brought in some pieces to show what would be sold at the kiosk, "I thought it was sturdy cotton pieces. In fact, I wrote that the use would be to sell organic cotton items."

To avoid any controversy, Ms. Castor said, mall officials considered renaming the business. "Everything she has we'll inspect to make sure it has no marijuana designs or even labels," she said.

"Anita is a very nice lady," she added. "If she had given any sign that she and her partner were going to be promoting drugs or anything like that, I wouldn't have written the lease."

The confusion between industrial hemp and the hemp used to produce marijuana has sent actor - and former Midlander - Woody Harrelson to jail for his efforts to promote the use of industrial hemp. He was arrested in Kentucky in June 1996 for planting four industrial hemp seeds - a misdemeanor - and released on $2,000 bail.

Ms. Teinert defends the plant as having been used for many years to make products such as rope and sails.

"It's extremely durable," she said. "One of its good qualities is that it's a very durable fabric."

She pointed out that Thomas Jefferson in his "Farm Book" referred to hemp uses and that it was one of the sturdiest plants known to American immigrants from Europe.

She said Jefferson knew that industrial hemp produced energetic, vigorous crops that choked out weeds and were protected by a pungent insect-resistant resin. In addition, unlike other crops such as cotton, industrial hemp replenishes soil nutrients without the need for herbicides or pesticides.

In 1942, Ms. Teinert adds, the Department of Agriculture produced a film encouraging American farmers to grow hemp for the war effort.

It's most popular use is in clothing such as jeans, shirts, dresses, jackets and footwear and accessories such as watchbands, belts and caps, all of which Teinert said is popular with young people today. Other products include hacky sacks, surfboards, bath mitts and coffee filters.

The industry is working to develop uses such as using hemp fiber as a substitute for plastic in auto dashboards and in the production of paper products to help preserve forests. The industry is also working to improve the quality of textiles, food-grade seed, seed oil, cosmetics and other industrial applications.

"Industrial hemp is not smoked for medical, recreational or any other reason," Ms. Teinert said, adding that she was surprised that her business had drawn such concern.

"I find a lot of the T-shirts mall stores sell offensive with skeletons on them," she said. "I wouldn't buy their product but I wouldn't boycott their stores, either. A lot of the lyrics on CDs I find offensive but they're played on the radio and the kids buy them. I wouldn't go into the record stores and raise a fuss."
